text: You use a simple rain gauge to measure rain so you catch the precipitation in a funnel and send it into a cylindrical tube. The gauge is set up so that the collection opening is much bigger than the inner tube. That difference functions as an amplifier. Like, if the opening is ten times the area of the measuring tube, an inch of rain will fill the tube ten inches high. This magnification lets observers read small amounts, like hundredths of an inch, accurately. Its not perfect. A big source of errors is evaporation, water quickly evaporates before you even see it, in warm and windy conditions. Another major source of error is wind exposure. It's a common problem. The wind makes a lot of turbulence around the mouth and pushes the raindrops over the opening and the gauge will under-estimate the rainfall.
